title: Define it
hook: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, as it is (Meditations 3.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday: only now. Your line was only this. When your mind ran ahead or behind, did one breath bring it back? Day five hundred forty-six, the end of a week.

A worry rarely arrives in plain words. It arrives as a cloud. Something about money. Something about that test result. Something about the way she said goodnight. It's big and blurry and it fills the room. Now try to write it down in one flat sentence, the way a clerk would. Sometimes the cloud shrinks the moment it has edges. Marcus Aurelius used this trick on himself, and wrote down exactly how it works. Today: define it.
screen: `A WORRY ARRIVES AS A CLOUD.` → `WRITE IT LIKE A CLERK.` → `DEFINE IT.`

segments.voice: First, the method. The eleventh entry of book three opens by calling this one more aid to add to the others. Marcus writes: always make a definition, or a description, of whatever presents itself to your mind. See what it is in its substance, stripped bare, whole, and tell yourself its name, and the names of the parts it's made of. Second, why bare. Marcus's point is that what upsets us is often less the thing than the coat we put on it. A late bill becomes I'm failing at life. A curt email becomes they're about to fire me. Defining strips the coat off. A late bill is a piece of paper asking for an amount by a date. That may still be a problem, but now it's a problem you can see. Third, the questions. Marcus goes on to ask of each thing: what is it, what is it made of, how long will it last, and what does it ask of me? Gentleness, courage, truth, faithfulness, simplicity? A defined thing points to a response. A cloud just points to dread. He says nothing so enlarges the mind as being able to examine everything that happens methodically and truly. Fourth, the week. Look at what this week has built. While I can: the mind won't last forever. Could I say it: think only what you could say out loud. Nothing better: the four goods. Keep faith: your word. Judge carefully: the power that forms opinions. Only this: the present. And now, as it is. Seven short lines, each small enough to say in one breath.
screen: `MAKE A DEFINITION OF EACH THING.` · `STRIP OFF THE COAT.` · `WHAT IS IT, WHAT DOES IT ASK OF ME?` · `SEVEN SHORT LINES.` · then, large: `AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring up one worry that's been sitting with you. Let it be a cloud for a moment. Now describe it plainly, as a clerk would, in one flat sentence. No adjectives, no predictions. What is it, actually? What is it made of? How long will it last? Then ask Marcus's last question: what does it ask of me? Patience, a phone call, courage? Notice the size of it now. The bell holds the time.
Define it. Marcus's method: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, name it and its parts, and ask what it asks of you. Today's word.
Your line: as it is. When something upsets you today, say it back to yourself in one flat sentence, as it is, before you react. Day five hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 3.11 by writing a worry down in one plain sentence, naming what it is and what it asks of them, before deciding how to respond.

match.prompt: as it is — tap the pairs.
pairs: what we add to the bare thing
what does it ask of me?

myth: Marcus says to describe things in vivid, emotional terms
he says to see them stripped bare, and name them and their parts.
Marcus asks of each thing how long it will last
it's one of his questions, with what it is and what it asks of me.
Marcus says defining things plainly makes the mind smaller
he says nothing so enlarges the mind as examining things methodically and truly.

fork.setup: on the drive to work, your car starts making a new grinding noise. your mind fills with storm clouds. what fits 3.11?
options: imagine every way it could go wrong.
describe it plainly: a new noise, from the front, when braking.
turn up the radio and ignore it.
fork.reveal: Marcus defines the thing bare: a noise, with a place and a time. what it asks of you, for now, is a call to a mechanic and some patience.

original.note: Greek, 'appearance, impression': in Stoic language, what presents itself to the mind before we judge it.

trapdoor: what it means: strip each thing to its bare substance, name its parts, and ask what it asks of you.
what a scholar hears: the Stoics worked with the phantasia, the impression; defining it plainly is how assent is kept honest.
recall: blood, bones, a net of nerves

notes: 3.11 paraphrased: make a definition or description of the thing presented, to see what it is in substance, in its nudity, as a whole; tell yourself its name and the names of its components; nothing is so productive of magnanimity as to examine methodically and truly all that presents itself; ask what it is, what it is composed of, how long it will last, and what virtue it needs from me (gentleness, manliness, truth, fidelity, simplicity, contentment). Confirm.
Week look-back lists the carries of days 540–546 (while I can, could I say it, nothing better, keep faith, judge carefully, only this, as it is).
'Courage' stands in for Long's 'manliness' (Greek andreia); confirm acceptable.

Editor review (2026-10-01): fixed the false claim that 'Marcus is assembling a toolkit, one tool a day' (the path assembles it; 3.11 itself calls the method one more aid) and changed the week head, which also clashed with tomorrow's 'tools ready'; 'most of what upsets us' attributed to Marcus and softened; cut the speculative 'a man who needed it'; replaced the manager-message fork, which repeated day 544's unanswered-message fork; 'often' to 'some'.
